claims.text: Melt-spinning can provide cooling rates approaching 10^6 K/s for phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
An ultrafast quench followed by a brief controlled thermal-relaxation step will improve glass-forming ability relative to conventional slower cooling.
An ultrafast quench followed by a brief controlled thermal-relaxation step will delay crystallization onset relative to conventional slower cooling.
At fixed Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 composition, rapid melt-spinning produces an amorphous structure whereas slower cooling produces crystalline or multiphase structures.
Cooling at approximately 3018 K/s produces fewer phases than slow cooling at approximately 52 K/s in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The proposed intervention is not expected to provide a benefit when the cooling rate is too low.
The proposed intervention may cease to be beneficial if the alloy chemistry deviates substantially from the baseline composition.
Ultrafast cooling minimizes atomic mobility during solidification.
Ultrafast cooling limits phase separation and crystalline nucleation.
The combined process produces a more homogeneous and defect-minimized amorphous structure.
The combined process reduces the number of nucleation sites available for crystallization.
A brief post-quench thermal-relaxation step permits subtle atomic rearrangement without triggering crystallization.
The relaxed, low-nucleation-site amorphous structure will have greater thermal stability.
The combined protocol will produce a higher amorphous fraction upon solidification than slower cooling.
The combined protocol will increase the crystallization-onset temperature measured by DSC.
Phosphorus addition and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability in the studied Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-P alloy.
Excessive post-quench thermal relaxation may trigger partial crystallization.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in both amorphous content and crystallization-onset temperature relative to a slower-cooled control would falsify the hypothesis.
